topics: 📢 Thirty, Sixty, or Ninety Days? — Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and the Rabbis on proclamation length
🗓️ Consecutive Days vs. Market Days — reconciling 'thirty days' with 'sixty days' for the same halakha
💸 When Does the Court Touch Orphans' Property? — Rav Asi's interest-only rule vs. Rabbi Yoḥanan's added ketubah
⚖️ Why the Court Normally Holds Back — three different reasons: an unobligated mitzva, a hidden receipt, a lost payment slip
📜 Rava's Final Ruling — specified bequests need no steward, unspecified ones do, and the Neharde'ans push back

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Selling Orphans' Land and Consecrated Property
overview.subtitle: Arakhin 22a–22b
overview.hebrewSource: שׁוּם הַיְּתוֹמִים שְׁלֹשִׁים יוֹם, וְשׁוּם הַהֶקְדֵּשׁ שִׁשִּׁים יוֹם, דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי מֵאִיר
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf opens with a three-way tannaitic dispute over exactly how many days the court must proclaim a sale of orphans' land or consecrated property before selling it, and a story of Rav Ḥisda getting the transmission of this halakha wrong more than once. The Gemara then asks a deeper question: when is the court even permitted to sell a minor orphan's inherited property to pay their late father's debts? Rav Asi limits it to interest-accruing loans; Rabbi Yoḥanan adds a wife's marriage contract. A long sequence of proofs and rejections follows, testing both positions against mishnayot and baraitot, before the Gemara settles on the operative halakha and Rava's final, more nuanced ruling about specified versus unspecified bequests.

slides.title: 📢 How Long Must the Proclamation Run?
slides.subtitle: A three-way tannaitic dispute, with a halakhic ruling for orphans' land

callout.label: Confused transmission:
callout.text: When Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Avin repeated this halakha, Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak had to press him twice — sixty or thirty? orphans or consecrated property? in accordance with Rabbi Meir or Rabbi Yehuda? — since Rabbi Meir himself says thirty, not sixty, for orphans.

slides.title: 🗓️ Resolving the Contradiction: Consecutive Days vs. Market Days
slides.subtitle: Avimi's explanation, which spared Rav Ḥisda much frustration

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rav Ḥisda: 'I absorbed many blows from Avimi over this halakha' before understanding it
2️⃣ If the proclamation runs on consecutive days, it follows Rabbi Meir's count: thirty days
3️⃣ If it runs only on Monday and Thursday — market days, when villagers gather and courts convene — it takes sixty days to complete
4️⃣ Even though that's really only eighteen actual announcement-days, stretching it over sixty days ensures word spreads widely enough

slides.title: 💸 When May the Court Sell Orphans' Property?
slides.subtitle: Rav Asi and Rabbi Yoḥanan set different thresholds

boxes.title: Rav Asi
items: Only if the debt is accruing interest that would consume the estate
Otherwise: wait until the orphans reach majority
No allowance made for a wife's ketubah — her labor is already assigned to the orphans in exchange for support

boxes.title: Rabbi Yoḥanan
items: A wife's marriage contract — because her ongoing sustenance (mezonot) from the estate is a real, mounting loss
Applies once she claims her ketubah in court (after which she loses further sustenance anyway)

callout.label: Later dispute:
callout.text: Mareimar collected a divorced woman's ketubah from orphans' property; Ravina objected that Rabbi Yoḥanan's ketubah leniency applies only to a widow (who costs the estate ongoing mezonot), not a divorced woman. Ameimar answered: even Rabbi Yoḥanan's reason is really 'for her favor' (so she can remarry) — which applies equally to both.

slides.title: ⚖️ Why Does the Court Usually Hold Back?
slides.subtitle: Three amora'im, three different reasons for the same reluctance

lines.speaker: Rav Pappa
lines.text: Repaying a creditor is a mitzva — and minor orphans are not yet obligated to perform mitzvot, so the court cannot act in their place.

lines.speaker: R' Huna b. Yeh.
lines.text: The concern is practical: the father may have secretly handed the creditor bundles of coins before he died, and we simply don't know.

lines.speaker: Rava
lines.text: Similarly practical: perhaps the father already paid and received a receipt (shovar) that the orphans don't know exists.

lines.speaker: R' Huna b. Yeh.
lines.text: But we don't worry about a hidden receipt elsewhere — a wife or creditor overseas can still collect via oath!

lines.speaker: Rava
lines.text: That's different — there, the concern is to stop people from fleeing overseas to dodge their creditors, not a receipt.

callout.label: Practical difference:
callout.text: Between Rav Pappa and Rav Huna: if the debtor admitted the debt, or died while excommunicated for non-payment, Rav Huna's concern evaporates and the court acts; for Rav Pappa the orphans' non-obligation still blocks it. The halakha follows Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua.

slides.title: 📜 Rava's Final Ruling on Repaying a Father's Debt
slides.subtitle: The default rule, its override, and whether a steward is appointed
rows: Standard unpaid debt, no special instruction
Father said: 'Give this field / these 100 dinars to so-and-so'
No — the gift is already specified
Yes — to protect the orphans' best land
Sages of Neharde'a: in all these cases
Yes, except when a field is found to be stolen — then it's simply returned

summary.principle: A sale of orphans' or consecrated property must be publicly proclaimed for a set period (thirty or sixty days, by the strict count of consecutive vs. market days), and the court sells a deceased father's property to satisfy his debts only in limited circumstances — never freely, out of concern for the orphans' unfulfilled obligations, a hidden payment, or a lost receipt.

flowSteps.content: 📢 Proclamation length disputed: Rabbi Meir (30/60), Rabbi Yehuda (60/90), Rabbis (60/60) — halakha: 60 days for orphans
🗓️ Reconciled: 30 consecutive days = 60 days counted only on market days (Monday/Thursday)

columns.content: 💸 Rav Asi: only interest-bearing debts trigger a sale; Rabbi Yoḥanan adds a wife's ketubah
⚖️ Rav Pappa, Rav Huna, and Rava each give a different reason the court normally refrains

flowSteps.content: 📜 Rava's ruling: no sale for a plain debt; yes if the father specified the gift (no steward) or left it vague (steward appointed)
🎓 Key Principle: minor orphans' property is protected by default — the court intervenes only where real loss, a father's explicit word, or halakha demands it

quiz.q: According to Avimi's resolution, how can the halakha be 'sixty days' for orphans' property when Rabbi Meir explicitly says 'thirty days'?
o: Avimi simply rejected Rabbi Meir's opinion entirely
Thirty days refers to consecutive daily proclamations; sixty days refers to proclaiming only on Monday and Thursday market days
The sixty-day count applies only to consecrated property, never to orphans
It was a scribal error in the baraita
quiz.e: Avimi explained that Rabbi Meir's 'thirty days' is for consecutive daily announcements, while announcing only on the twice-weekly market days (Monday and Thursday) stretches the same effective exposure over sixty days.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between Rav Asi's and Rabbi Yoḥanan's positions on when the court may sell orphans' property to pay their father's debts?
o: They fully agree with no difference
Rav Asi allows it only for interest-accruing debts; Rabbi Yoḥanan also allows it for a wife's marriage contract, due to her ongoing sustenance loss
Rav Asi allows it for any debt; Rabbi Yoḥanan restricts it to interest-bearing debts only
Both permit it only for gentile creditors
quiz.e: Rav Asi limits court action to interest-bearing loans that would erode the estate, while Rabbi Yoḥanan adds a wife's ketubah claim, reasoning that her continued sustenance from the estate is a real ongoing loss to the orphans.

quiz.q: What reason does Rav Pappa give for why the court generally does not attend to minor orphans' property to repay a debt?
o: The orphans might dispute the debt's validity
Repaying a creditor is a mitzva, and minor orphans are not yet obligated to perform mitzvot
Orphans' property can never legally be sold
The debt is automatically forgiven upon the debtor's death
quiz.e: Rav Pappa's reasoning is that repayment of a debt is a religious obligation (mitzva), and since minor orphans are not bound by mitzvot, the court cannot compel this act through their property.

quiz.q: What is the practical difference between Rav Pappa's reasoning and Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua's reasoning for why the court withholds orphans' property?
o: There is no practical difference between them

When the debtor admitted the debt or died excommunicated for non-payment, Rav Huna's concern (a hidden payment) disappears and the court acts, but Rav Pappa's reasoning (orphans aren't obligated in mitzvot) still blocks collection
Rav Pappa's reasoning only applies to gentile creditors
Rav Huna's reasoning only applies to consecrated property
quiz.e: If the debtor admitted owing the money, or died while excommunicated for non-payment, there is no more doubt about the debt, removing Rav Huna's concern about a hidden payment — but Rav Pappa's concern about the orphans' non-obligation in mitzvot still applies regardless.

quiz.q: According to Rava's final ruling, when the father specified 'give this field to so-and-so' before he died, does the court appoint a steward (apotropos) for the orphans?
o: Yes, always, regardless of specification
No — because the gift is already specific, there is nothing for a steward to negotiate or protect
Only if the field is worth more than the debt
A steward is appointed only for consecrated property, never for private debts
quiz.e: Rava rules that when the bequest is already specified ('this field,' 'these 100 dinars'), the court attends to the property but does not appoint a steward, since there is no ambiguity to manage — unlike an unspecified bequest, where a steward protects the orphans' best land.
